SCOTLAND 2 NORTH MACEDONIA 1: John McGinn at the double to spare the blushes of Pocognoli's shaky Scots on skipper Robertson's substantial night

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dailymail

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.
  • Published: 17:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 17:11 EST, 13 November 2026.
  • On the night when the nation looked over its shoulder and celebrated the past, the here and now for Scotland looked distinctly uncertain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:01 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 17:11 EST, 13 November 2026.

On the night when the nation looked over its shoulder and celebrated the past, the here and now for Scotland looked distinctly uncertain.

Coming 40 years and a day after his friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish, pulled on a Scotland jersey for the 102nd and final time, Andy Robertson joined the great man on a mark which, for years, seemed beyond the reach of mere mortals.

By time up, history had mercifully repeated itself at Hampden. Back in the day, Dalglish, by then player-manager at Anfield, sailed into the international sunset on the back of a routine 3-0 win over Luxembourg.

Facing another opponent of modest ability, Robertson’s red letter day didn’t go quite as smoothly. Yet, when the Tottenham man is old and grey and reflecting on the night he created history, the annals will at least record a slender victory.

While his side did just about enough to prevail here, this was another fraught night for Sebastien Pocognoli.

Recent findings suggest that you can talk about the need for patience under the new manager until the cows come home. But North Macedonia are 71st in FIFA’s rankings. Scotland are 43rd.

John McGinn celebrates in trademark fashion after netting Scotland's winner from the spot.

At Hampden Park, in front of an expectant crowd, Scotland should be putting them to the sword with something to spare.

Yet, for long enough, the Belgian’s latest-look side were flat, predictable and plodding. It said much that it took the intervention of VAR for them to get the penalty which would ultimately lead to three points being accrued.

John McGinn’s second half double saved the Belgian’s blushes and truthfully there was little else to get the Tartan Army off their seats.

Industry observers note that too many massive-name players scarcely merited pass marks. Too few looked comfortable in the system the manager is trying to bed in.

If it was a step in the right direction, it was a small one. After five games under the affable Belgian, the progress has certainly not been startling.

While it goes without saying that beating the Swiss in St Gallen on Monday will be an inordinately tougher task, having some hope of moving up a place and securing a kinder draw for the Euros is still better than no hope.

Regardless of what pot they end up in when the draw is made in Belfast next month, a radical improvement will certainly be required across the board if they are to stand any chance of qualifying for the tournament via the front door.

As well as the achievements of Robertson and Dalglish, the career of Craig Gordon was acknowledged before the match with the 84-times capped keeper deservedly afforded a warm hand by the Tartan Army.

McGinn slots home his penalty after Ben Gannon-Doak had been brought down in the area.

There were absolutely no excuses for Scotland here. North Macedonia were a tier-two team in name only. They arrived at Hampden having not won in 12 matches and not scored in eight.

Another Pocognoli game saw another back-three combination. This time Luke Graham was selected in the centre of the unit with Ryan Porteous and Kieran Tierney deployed either side of the Stoke man in what were their first appearances under the Belgian.

Industry observers note that robertson and Ben Gannon-Doak were tasked with providing the width in the 3-4-3. Scott McTominay slotted back into an advanced role beside John McGinn with the returning Che Adams asked to lead the line.

For all there was a healthy crowd in excess of 40,000 inside Hampden, the atmosphere was subdued. In the four Nations League games to date under the latest manager, the side hadn’t exactly given the supporters much to feed off.

In a recent development, despite some significant guns returning, Scotland made a laboured start to their night’s work. It said much that Graham, on his second appearance, was busier than any defender in white.

The first opening came as a result of an opposition error. John McGinn found Billy Gilmour who fed the overlapping Robertson. The skipper’s cross was well out of Adams’ reach.

Sebastien Pocognoli got his first Hampden win as Scotland boss but it was a nervy night.

Although Ljupche Doriev worried Angus Gunn with a curling effort, Scotland began to exert some degree of control on the match. Lewis Ferguson kept the visitors hemmed in with a header into McTominay’s feet. The Napoli man saw his shot on the spin well saved by Stole Dimitrievski.

Pocognoli was frustrated when Slovakian referee Michal Ocenas blew for a foul on McTominay, his justifiable gripe being that playing an advantage would have seen Robertson have a crack at goal.

Dimitrievski had a decent night. Although Adams’ flashing header from McGinn’s corner took a deflection, a reflex save at his near post added to Scotland’s frustration.

According to recent reports, north Macedonia were a spirited but ordinary side. They still had enough to thwart Pocognoli’s men.

Sources indicate that gannon-Doak saw plenty of the ball down the right, yet the end product often wasn’t there. The Bournemouth man did tee up Billy Gilmour for one dangerous cross. McTominay tried to replicate his iconic overhead kick against Denmark nearly a year ago. This time, his aim wasn’t true.

You could hardly blame Pocognoli’s star man for failing to find the net on that occasion.

Scott McTominay attempts an overhead spectacular a year on from THAT goal at Hampden.

Recent findings suggest that that wasn’t the case a few moments later when Adams slipped him in. Dimitrievski saved McTominay’s strike with an outstretched leg when he should have been picking the ball out of his net.

Adams had just blazed a strike high over the top while one-on-one with the keeper although the offside flag saved his blushes.

It has been revealed that the visitors came closer to edging ahead when Eljif Elmas played the pass of the match over Scotland’s static defence to pick out Ezgjan Alioski. His lay-off was smashed into the side net by Enis Bardhi.

It has been revealed that A wholly uninspiring first-half concluded with Robertson advancing up the left and launching a cross halfway to Castlemilk. This was not going well.

Pocognoli waited on the edge of the pitch for his players returning, his enthusiastic applause clearly audible in the arena.

His hopes of a breakthrough at the outset of the second period were dashed in extraordinary fashion. Adams did well to chase a ball down to the line and cut it back. McTominay and his marker couldn’t connect, leaving Gilmour the simple task of firing into an unguarded net. Leaning back, his failure to even hit the target was unfathomable.

Elmin Rastoder celebrates after silencing Hampden with a leveller for North Macedonia.

Within seconds, the sense of relief inside Hampden was palpable as the opener finally arrived. Porteous got enough distance on his clearing header for Adams to barge Visar Musliu out of the way.

McGinn was alert to the situation and burst into the box. His crisp strike finally had the beating of the goalkeeper.

Sources indicate that it should have settled Pocognoli’s side and paved the way for a comfortable result. Instead, they were pegged back within three minutes.

Sources indicate that it was all just so simple and so avoidable. Bardhi’s whipped corner only needed McTominay to outjump his man. Flat-footed as the delivery arrived, he could only watch on in horror as Elmin Rastoder’s flashing header beat Angus Gunn.

Recent findings suggest that although Gilmour worked the keeper with a low strike, North Macedonia also sniffed a second goal. Time and time again, they got into pockets of space on the flanks and fired in dangerous crosses.

Adams made way for Oli McBurnie, the Hull man desperately hoping for his first goal on his 21st international appearance. He had a gilt-edged chance to get off the mark when rolled in by McGinn, but selflessly passed to the overlapping Gannon-Doak.

Scotland move on to their final game away in Switzerland as they look to finish on a high note.

Sources indicate that the winger appeared to take a heavy touch which allowed the keeper to rescue the situation. VAR, however, spotted that Dimitrievski had impeded him. Penalty.

McGinn did the necessary from 12 yards, smashing the ball straight down the middle for his 24th international goal.

North Macedonia, to their credit, kept going for it. They sensed a fragility in Scotland. Everyone in the ground could.

McGinn’s calm conversion proved to be just about enough to get the job done. But it’s fair to suggest that we are still awaiting lift-off in the latest era.

SCOTLAND (3-4-1-2): Gunn; Porteous, Graham, Tierney; Gannon-Doak (Hickey 76), Ferguson, Gilmour (Christie 76), Robertson; McGinn; Adams (McBurnie 67), McTominay. Booked: Ferguson. Manager: Sebastien Pocognoli.

Sources indicate that NORTH MACEDONIA (4-2-3-1): Dimitrievski; Ilievski, Mladenovski, Musliu, Alioski; Gashtarov (Elezi 64), Elmas (Stankovski 78); Churlinov (Maleski 64), Bardhi, Doriev (Nikolov 85); Rastoder. Booked: None. Manager: Goce Sedloski.

Referee: Michal Ocenas (Slovakia).

#2495. Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics

Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 49 min read (9808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~49 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Aggressive scaling in silicon electronics—although essential for improving power, performance, area and cost—faces increasing challenges in further reducing power consumption due to electrostatic and leakage constraints1,2.
  • Modern silicon transistors continue to improve with technological advancement.
  • It has been revealed that the sizable bandgaps of 2D semiconductors suppress off-state current, while their atomically thin van der Waals (vdW) structure enables excellent gate control, making them well suited for energy-efficient operation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aggressive scaling in silicon electronics—although essential for improving power, performance, area and cost—faces increasing challenges in further reducing power consumption due to electrostatic and leakage constraints1,2. Achieving efficient operation at low supply voltages therefore requires upcoming materials and gate-stack engineering strategies. Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors offer intrinsic advantages because their atomic thickness affords excellent gate control, and their sizable bandgaps suppress off-state current. However, a major obstacle is the imperfect interface between 2D channels and gate dielectrics, which degrades subthreshold swing, hysteresis and bias-temperature instability3. Here we demonstrate that a wafer-scale, transferable, single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric can be van der Waals integrated with 2D transition metal dichalcogenides. The obtained pristine 2D-dielectric interface enables subthreshold swing close to the thermal limit, record-low hysteresis and well-matched transfer characteristics for both n- and p-type enhancement-mode field-effect transistors. Building on this, we demonstrate complementary field-effect transistors, whose inverters achieve high voltage gain and large noise margins with subpicowatt static power consumption. These results highlight the promise of 2D semiconductors for ultra-low-power operation.

Modern silicon transistors continue to improve with technological advancement. However, as scaling progresses, power efficiency has emerged as a critical constraint, especially for ultra-low-energy applications such as wearable electronics, implantable medical devices, Internet of Things (IoT) nodes, edge AI processors and distributed sensor networks. To achieve substantial power reductions, device operation at reduced supply voltages has been explored extensively4,5. Nevertheless, silicon’s relatively small bandgap inherently increases leakage, while maintaining strong electrostatic control at scaled dimensions remains challenging6. A recent simulation study that compares silicon transistors with planar 2D field-effect transistors (FETs) from 16 nm to 1 nm technology nodes highlighted the low-power potential of 2D FET-based circuits7. These observations motivate the investigation of 2D semiconductors for low-power operation8,9,10,11,12.

It has been revealed that the sizable bandgaps of 2D semiconductors suppress off-state current, while their atomically thin van der Waals (vdW) structure enables excellent gate control, making them well suited for energy-efficient operation. Proof-of-concept inverters assembled from n- and p-type 2D semiconductors—including MoS2-WSe2 (refs. 13,14,15), MoS2-MoTe2 (ref. 16) and pseudo-complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) based on single transition metal dichalcogenides (TMD)17—have demonstrated low-voltage and subthreshold operation with reduced static power consumption (Extended Data Table 1). However, these demonstrations rely on non-scalable approaches, such as mechanically exfoliated flakes or lateral assembly of dissimilar materials and devices. Their voltage gains are also limited (Extended Data Table 1), primarily because of asymmetric n-channel FET (n-FET) and p-channel FET (p-FET) transfer characteristics. One major source of this asymmetry is the gate stack: an imperfect 2D/high-κ interface degrades subthreshold swing, whereas unintentional dielectric-induced doping shifts the threshold voltage (Vth), impairing inverter performance. Most critically, WSe2-based p-FETs often have pronounced bipolar transfer characteristics, which are incompatible with robust CMOS operation and integration. High-permittivity, crystalline dielectric or buffer layers have been used to improve gate controllability by increasing gate capacitance and suppressing defect-induced degradation18,19,20. Clean vdW integration of gate dielectrics with 2D semiconductors also minimizes interfacial traps caused by direct deposition processes21,22,23,24. Despite these advances, a scalable method for achieving pristine 2D/high-κ interfaces in both n- and p-type transistors remains elusive.

Here we show that standard amorphous HfO2 grown by atomic layer deposition (ALD) contains prevalent charge traps that degrade WSe2 FETs by inducing unwanted bipolar transport, pronounced hysteresis, and compromised n- and p-type performance. Transitioning to a single-crystal dielectric mitigates these complications. Although crystalline dielectrics retain structural imperfections, their threading dislocations are spatially confined to one-dimensional defects with self-passivated cores, making them less detrimental to two-dimensional interfacial transport. We fabricated a -3-inch free-standing single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide (A-TiO2) membrane, a high-κ dielectric with κ ≈ 44–50 at a thickness of 18.2 nm. Patterned membranes are van-der-Waals-integrated with 2D semiconductors as top- or bottom-gate dielectrics, preserving pristine 2D/high-κ interfaces. The resulting MoS2 n-FETs and WSe2 p-FETs have ideal unipolar behaviour, well-matched enhancement-mode thresholds, near-ideal subthreshold swing and record-low hysteresis. Complementary inverters deliver high voltage gain, wide noise margins and record-low static power (subpicowatt) at low voltage. Furthermore, non-equilibrium Green’s function (NEGF) simulations show that this architecture is scalable to a gate length (Lg) of 10 nm, comparable with the 1 nm technology-node specifications in the IRDS 2031 roadmap while maintaining stable operation at 0.3 V.

We use a laser scanning-assisted pulsed-laser deposition technique to fabricate free-standing 3-inch A-TiO2 dielectric layers (Methods). In brief, a SrTiO3 layer was first epitaxially grown on a 3-inch single-crystalline LaAlO3 (001) substrate, followed by a water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 sacrificial layer that served as a template for the subsequent epitaxial growth of single-crystal A-TiO2 dielectric layers. The optical image of the as-grown 3-inch LaAlO3//SrTiO3//Sr3Al2O6//A-TiO2 heterostructure and its cross-sectional high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image profile with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) elemental mappings are shown in Fig. 1a,b. To enable wafer-scale vdW integration with 2D semiconductors, we develop a transfer process as schematically illustrated in Fig. 1c. The grown heterostructure is patterned into 100 × 100 μm2 squares using inductively coupled plasma etching to expose the underlying Sr3Al2O6 layer surrounding the defined squares. The sacrificial Sr3Al2O6 layer is then selectively removed by immersion in deionized water, leaving the A-TiO2 layer in direct contact with the LaAlO3//SrTiO3 substrate. Owing to the vdW interaction between A-TiO2 and the substrate, the 3-inchpatterned A-TiO2 can be lifted off using a polymer support layer and transferred onto target substrates. Acetone washing followed by a mild O2 plasma treatment was used to remove polymer residues from the transferred A-TiO2. A photograph of the as-released 3-inch A-TiO2 layer on a Si//SiO2 substrate is shown in Fig. 1d.

Uniformity and flatness of the gate dielectric are critical for 2D semiconductor devices. The thickness mapping of the transferred 3-inch A-TiO2 film (Supplementary Fig. 1) indicates the exceptionally low coefficient of variation of 1.15%. The thickness of the transferred A-TiO2 membrane is further supported by atomic force microscopy (AFM; Supplementary Fig. 2) and X-ray reflectometry (Supplementary Fig. 3) measurements. Meanwhile, the AFM image of the A-TiO2 transferred onto SiO2 reveals an atomically flat surface, with a minimum average roughness (Ra) of approximately 0.12 nm and an average roughness of 0.13 nm across the 3-inch A-TiO2 platform (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Fig. 1d). Furthermore, AFM measurements support that the surface roughness for all thickness variants remains ≤0.2 nm (Supplementary Fig. 4). This roughness is comparable with that of atomically flat hexagonal boron nitride (around 0.19 nm), highlighting the exceptional smooth nature25,26. Reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) of the as-grown LaAlO3//SrTiO3//Sr3Al2O6//A-TiO2 heterostructure indicate coherent single-crystalline growth (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). Azimuthal X-ray diffraction ϕ scanning along the (110) plane of free-standing A-TiO2 with different thicknesses further supported in-plane single-crystallinity without rotated domains (Extended Data Fig. 1c). The localized crystallinity is revealed by plan-view dark-field TEM imaging and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) analysis (Fig. 1f), both of which support the local atomic-scale lattice registry and phase purity. X-ray diffraction characterization supports the single-crystalline quality of the A-TiO2 films. The symmetric (004) and asymmetric (107) rocking curves of the released A-TiO2 yield a screw dislocation density of 3.8 × 109 cm−2 and an edge dislocation density of 2 × 1010 cm−2, respectively (Methods). This dislocation density, which arises from the lattice mismatch inherent to the current sacrificial substrate, represents a lower bound for device performance that we expect to substantially improve by migrating to more closely lattice-matched systems. Moreover, asymmetric (107) reciprocal space mapping corroborates the structural homogeneity by tracking the strain state evolution post-release and verifying the absence of polycrystalline domains (Supplementary Fig. 5)27,28,29.

It has been revealed that the metal–insulator–metal (MIM) capacitor structure is used to evaluate the capacitance of the as-prepared freestanding A-TiO2, where the A-TiO2 layer is transferred onto a gold-coated silicon substrate followed by the deposition of a top titanium/gold electrode (Extended Data Fig. 2). The inset of Fig. 1g demonstrates the dependence of the effective permittivity (εeff) on thickness, where each data point represents an average value obtained from multiple capacitors of the corresponding A-TiO2 thickness. Notably, the extracted εeff reflects the combined electrostatic contribution from both the single-crystal A-TiO2 layer and the interfacial vdW gap layer formed at the transferred interfaces. The effective value εeff is related to the measured capacitance (Ceff) through \({C}_{\mathrm{eff}}=A{\varepsilon }_{0}{\varepsilon }_{\mathrm{eff}}/t\), where \(A\) is the area of the top electrodes, t is the thickness of the A-TiO2 layer and ε0 is the vacuum permittivity. The εeff as a function of thickness can be well described by the typical dead layer model emerging in a high-κ nanocapacitor18. Figure 1g further summarizes the thickness dependence of equivalent oxide thickness (EOT), calculated as \(3.9t/{\varepsilon }_{\mathrm{eff}}\). The EOT scales nearly linearly with the A-TiO2 thickness, indicating that sub-1-nm EOT values can be achieved with films thinner than 7.7 nm. Meanwhile, the capacitance-equivalent thickness (CET) was determined using metal–oxide-semiconductor capacitors (Supplementary Fig. 6), demonstrating that an approximately 7.2-nm-thick A-TiO2 film achieves a CET of approximately 1 nm.

Industry observers note that for practical device deployment, future high-κ dielectrics must simultaneously demonstrate minimal leakage current and high breakdown strength, for which single-crystal dielectrics represent a compelling high-κ solution for 2D electronics. Figure 1h shows the leakage current characteristics of the as-prepared A-TiO2 membranes with thicknesses of 5.8 nm and 18.2 nm. Both variants have excellent insulating behaviour, with leakage current densities (Jleak) remaining below the low-power limit (1.5 × 10−2 A cm–2) up to operating voltages of 1.5 V (2.6 MV cm–1) and 4.6 V (2.5 MV cm–1) for 5.8-nm and 18.2-nm A-TiO2, respectively. The breakdown field (Ebd) characteristics of the 5.8-nm and 18.2-nm A-TiO2 layers are statistically analysed in Fig. 1i. Furthermore, time-dependent dielectric breakdown analysis of A-TiO2 with an EOT ≈ 1.5 nm under constant-voltage stress projects a ten-year device lifetime at operating voltages below 4 V (Supplementary Fig. 7). These results demonstrate the suitability of transferred A-TiO2 for low-power electronic applications.

To examine the gate dielectric performance of A-TiO2 in 2D transistors, a 3-inch patterned A-TiO2 membrane is transferred onto an Si//SiO2 substrate incorporating patterned platinum back-gate electrodes (refer to Supplementary Fig. 8 for details on the fabrication process flow). A wafer-scale monolayer MoS2 (1L-MoS2) film grown by chemical vapour deposition (CVD) is subsequently transferred to the top of A-TiO2, where the quality of MoS2 is verified by Raman and photoluminescence spectroscopy (Supplementary Fig. 9). MoS2 channels are defined and contacted using antimony/gold metals to form local bottom-gate MoS2 FETs. Photographs of the 3-inch device array are shown in Fig. 2a,b, and a schematic of the device structure is presented in Fig. 2c. A cross-sectional HRTEM image at the contact area reveals two distinct vdW gaps at the 1L-MoS2/Sb and 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 interfaces (Fig. 2d). At the latter interface, the well-defined single-crystalline dielectric surface provides a clean interface contact with MoS2, minimizing charge-impurity scattering and doping. The clean interface is also attributed to the optimized transfer and polymer removal process (Methods). Furthermore, the vdW gap at the interface of the 2D materials and A-TiO2 also plays a key role in effectively suppressing fringing-induced barrier lowering caused by using high-κ dielectric, which in turn helps to mitigate drain-induced barrier lowering in scaled devices18. At the MoS2/Sb interface, a pristine and intimate contact free of metal-induced defects is observed30, enabling a low contact resistance of about 120 Ω μm, as extracted using the transfer length method from devices with channel lengths ranging from 80 nm to 0.8 μm (Supplementary Fig. 10).

Recent findings suggest that to assess transistor performance with A-TiO2 gate oxide, we measured 100 p- and 100 n-type devices across the wafer, randomly sampled from five representative regions (Supplementary Fig. 11), where the majority of devices have consistent electrical characteristics across the wafer. Devices were qualified by excluding those with abnormal Vth shifts, Ion/Ioff outside 106–5 × 107, or failed electrical characteristics. Figure 2e shows representative transfer characteristics (Ids – Vgs) of 80 qualified long-channel 1L-MoS2 FETs integrated with a 5.8-nm-thick A-TiO2 dielectric (EOT ≈ 0.88 nm; W/L = 2 μm/3 μm). The average subthreshold swing across the array is 68 mV dec–1, with the best device achieving 61 mV dec–1. Similarly, 84 qualified bilayer WSe2 (2L-WSe2) FETs (W/L = 2 μm/2 μm) with A-TiO2 dielectric show excellent performance (Fig. 2f), delivering average and minimum subthreshold swing values of 79 mV dec–1 and 65 mV dec–1, respectively. The subthreshold swing values as a function of Ids for selected 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 and 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 devices are presented in Supplementary Fig. 13. Statistical distributions of Ion/Ioff, subthreshold swing and Vth for the working p- and n-type transistors are summarized in Supplementary Fig. 12, with most n- and p-FETs (>98%) exhibiting over seven orders of magnitude in Ion/Ioff ratios, low gate leakage and minimal variation in Vth. Supplementary Fig. 14a and 14b further present representative transfer characteristics of 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs integrated with thicker A-TiO2 gate dielectrics (18.2 nm; EOT ≈ 1.5 nm). Supplementary Fig. 14c–f show the corresponding gate leakage currents for 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs with 18.2-nm and 5.8 nm A-TiO2 gate dielectrics, supporting that strong electrostatic control is maintained without increased leakage even under aggressive EOT scaling. Extended Data Fig. 3a compares the subthreshold swing versus EOT across various technologies using CVD-grown 2D channels. Extended Data Fig. 3b further compares Jleak at an applied gate voltage of 1 V for various gate-stack technologies with EOT or CET ≤ 1 nm. The A-TiO2 gate stack demonstrates low Jleak with sub-1-nm EOT, remaining well below the low-power limit (1.5 × 10−2 A cm−2). Recent studies have highlighted the trade-off between leakage-current suppression and electrostatic scaling in vdW-integrated 2D transistor interfaces31, and readers are referred to these works for broader discussions on EOT benchmarking and scaling considerations.

Industry observers note that we further fabricated short-channel bottom-gated 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs with channel lengths of about 50 nm to evaluate gate controllability at scaled dimensions. Even at this reduced channel length, both 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 and 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 devices exhibit near-ideal subthreshold swing (around 72 mV dec–1) and a high Ion/Ioff ratio (>108) without an increase in off-state current (Fig. 2g,h). The short-channel devices also have high Ion at Vds = 0.6 V. For the 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 configuration, Ion reaches 227 μA μm–1 at Vov = 0.6 V and 167 μA μm–1 at Vov = 0.4 V. Similarly, the 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 device demonstrates Ion values of 136 μA μm–1 (Vov = –0.6 V) and 86 μA μm–1 (Vov = –0.4 V) at a drain bias of –0.6 V, where Vov = Vgs − Vth denotes the gate-overdrive voltage. The corresponding output characteristics are shown in Fig. 2i. These results can be attributed to the superior gate-to-channel electrostatic control enabled by the A-TiO2 high-κ gate stack (Extended Data Fig. 4). Figure 2j benchmarks the subthreshold swing versus channel length (Lch) for reported short-channel 2D FETs using different dielectric technologies, highlighting that the subthreshold swing values achieved with A-TiO2 gate dielectric are among the lowest reported for CVD-grown MoS2 and WSe2 devices with similar structures. Supplementary Table 1 benchmarks devices using amorphous or single-crystal gate dielectrics with CVD-grown 2D TMD channel materials. The proposed A-TiO2 integration achieves a sub-1-nm EOT, a subthreshold swing of below 65 mV dec–1 and a high Ion, metrics which align with the requirements for low-power, high-performance logic applications.

According to recent reports, hysteresis in the transistor transfer characteristics is a critical metric of operational stability. Here we systematically compare 2D transistors integrated with single-crystalline A-TiO2 to those using amorphous HfO2 and Al2O3 gate dielectrics deposited by the ALD approach (Methods). Extended Data Fig. 5 displays the Ids – Vgs characteristics for different types of dielectrics under forward and reverse gate-voltage sweeps. The hysteresis width (ΔVH) of 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FETs reaches an exceptionally small value of around 1.5 mV at the sweeping frequency (f) of 0.028 Hz (f = 1/tsw, where tsw represents the total forward and backward sweeping time). The cyclostationary behavior of the 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FET is further detailed in Supplementary Fig. 15. The minimal variation observed between the initial and 100th measurement cycles supports the robustness of the gate stack and ensures that our hysteresis characterization is reliable for future device benchmarking32. For a fair comparison, ΔVH is normalized by EOT33,34. Figure 3a summarizes the statistical distribution of normalized ΔVH extracted from devices employing different dielectrics (Supplementary Fig. 16), where A-TiO2 has the smallest hysteresis value among all the tested devices. Supplementary Fig. 17 further shows normalized ΔVH as a function of sweep frequency for a representative 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FET measured under different gate sweeping ranges. The resulting hysteresis remains minimal across all measurement conditions, in sharp contrast to MoS2 transistors with conventional SiO2, Al2O3 or HfO2 gate dielectrics, which display pronounced hysteresis, particularly at low sweeping frequencies, due to slow charge trapping in oxide defect states35. Figure 3b benchmarks the normalized ΔVH of 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 FETs against literature values reported for a range of dielectric technologies. Notably, our unencapsulated devices achieve a normalized ΔVH of 0.5 mV nm–1, which not only outperforms those of unencapsulated 2D transistors but also demonstrates superior stability compared with channel-encapsulated devices. Furthermore, bias-temperature instability (BTI) measurements reinforce the stability of the 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 interface (Methods), revealing small threshold voltage shift (ΔVth) under both positive (ΔVth = 40 mV) and negative (ΔVth = 50 mV) gate bias stress (Supplementary Fig. 18). These results indicate the scarcity of border traps within the single-crystalline gate dielectric and a clean dielectric/2D semiconductor interface, even when integrated using conventional wet transfer technologies. Although the BTI of these 2D FETs currently exceeds that of established silicon technology3, further optimization of the interface and dielectric quality remains a clear path toward industrial parity.

In a recent development, the record-low hysteresis can be attributed to the clean channel–dielectric interface and crystalline dielectric with low concentration of traps, which together drastically suppress charge trapping to enable low hysteresis. The estimated interface trap density (Dit) is determined as approximately 5.74 × 1011 cm−2 eV−1, substantially lower than the values typically reported for devices incorporating CVD-grown MoS2 channels (Supplementary Table 2), although CVD-synthesized MoS2 inevitably contains point defects (1011–1012 cm–2) due to thermodynamic and growth chemistry constraints36. To understand the origin of hysteresis, we perform cross-sectional scanning tunneling microscope/spectroscopy (XSTM/S) measurements to directly probe the in-gap states in dielectric oxides (Supplementary Note 1). A representative XSTM topography of the metal–dielectric interface is shown in Fig. 3c, whereas spatially resolved XSTM-STS measurements acquired at sub-0.5 nm intervals from the interface into the dielectric are presented in Fig. 3d. Amorphous HfO2 has pronounced in-gap states near the band edges, particularly close to the interface, indicating a high density of charge-trapping centres. By contrast, no discernible in-gap states are detected in A-TiO2, supporting its intrinsically low trap density.

Moreover, current-mode deep-level transient spectroscopy (I-DLTS) reveals distinct trap characteristics at 1L-MoS2/dielectric interfaces (Fig. 3e). 1L-MoS2/HfO2 has a shallow trap (0.221 eV below Ec) with a large capture cross-section (σn = 1.40 × 10−13 cm2). Conversely, 1L-MoS2/A-TiO2 highlights a deeper trap at 0.293 eV below Ec with a capture cross-section that is three orders of magnitude smaller (σn = 6.40 × 10−17 cm2), substantially suppressing trapping (Supplementary Note 2). The close agreement between XSTM-STS and I-DLTS measurements indicates that shallow, Coulomb-attractive traps dominate the 1L-MoS2/HfO2 interface, whereas deeper, near-neutral traps in A-TiO2   exhibit substantially lower trapping probability. The influence of dielectric quality is further illustrated in Fig. 3f, which compares the transfer characteristics of WSe2 p-FETs fabricated with A-TiO2 and amorphous HfO2 gate dielectrics. The A-TiO2-gated device has clean unipolar p-type behaviour across the entire gate sweep; however, the HfO2-gated device shows pronounced bipolar transport, incompatible with robust CMOS operation. This contrast indicates that the bipolar response is linked to defect-induced Fermi-level modulation associated with in-gap states in the amorphous dielectric (Supplementary Note 3). These findings underscore the critical importance of using high-quality dielectrics with low-trap density to achieve stable, unipolar p-type operation in WSe2 FETs.

It has been revealed that the stable and high-performance A-TiO2-gated 2D FETs motivate us to further demonstrate their scalable vertical integration into complementary field-effect transistors (CFETs) (Fig. 4a). Fabrication begins with MoS2 n-FET arrays, using buried gold electrodes as source and drain contacts and single-crystalline A-TiO2 as the top-gate dielectric. A vertical CMOS architecture is then constructed by stacking 2L-WSe2/A-TiO2 p-FET arrays directly above the n-type tier, sharing a common Pt gate electrode. After vertically interconnecting the drain electrodes of n- and p-FETs through the via-metal, where the output voltage (Vout) is measured, the CFET inverters are realized (the schematic structure is shown in Fig. 4b; refer to Extended Data Fig. 6 for detailed fabrication steps). Figure 4c shows the cross-sectional HRTEM images acquired at the channel region of a representative CFET inverter, revealing uniformly flat layers with atomically sharp vdW interfaces between the 2D semiconductors and the A-TiO2 gate dielectrics. An overview cross-sectional HRTEM image of the complete CFET stack, illustrating the vertical alignment of the top p-FET and bottom n-FET tiers, is provided in Extended Data Fig. 7.

In a recent development, the transfer curves of the bottom n-FETs and top p-FETs (Lch = 1 μm) measured from 16 CFETs are shown in Fig. 4d, exhibiting nearly symmetric behavior and limited device-to-device variation. Note that the voltage transfer characteristic (VTC) curves shown for the CFET inverters exclude abnormal devices (Supplementary Note 4). The yield of the CFET inverters is approximately 50% (25 functional devices out of 50 fabricated devices) and requires further engineering improvement. The standard deviations of normalized Ion are 21.8% for the n-FETs and 23.9% for the p-FETs. The average Vth is 0.9 V for the n-FETs and −1.1 V for the p-FETs, confirming enhancement-mode operation for both device types, which is essential for low-power logic applications. Both n- and p-FETs have steep subthreshold slopes, indicating high transconductance ( gm, defined as the change in drain current with respect to gate voltage, ∆Ids/∆Vgs) and transconductance efficiency (gm/Ids), which are essential for achieving large voltage gain in CFET inverters. Consistently, both device types maintain Ion/Ioff ratios exceeding 107 over a range of Vds while preserving a minimum subthreshold swing of about 75 mV dec–1 (Supplementary Fig. 19), enabling efficient inverter operation at reduced supply voltage (Vdd) with low power consumption. Figure 4e displays representative VTCs of the CFET inverters, demonstrating excellent full-rail logic swing across a range of Vdd from 0.1 V to 1 V. The voltage gain increases progressively with Vdd, from 12 V/V at 0.25 V to a peak value of 89 V/V at 1 V. Remarkably, even at the minimum Vdd of 0.1 V, the inverter maintains a gain value exceeding the minimum threshold (1 V/V) for functional logic operation37, highlighting the potential of this CFET architecture for ultra-low-voltage, energy-efficient circuits. Supplementary Fig. 20 summarizes the voltage gain, static power consumption (Pstatic) and estimated noise margins (NML, low-level noise margin; NMH, high-level noise margin) as functions of Vdd, extracted from 16 individual CFET inverters. Owing to the crystalline nature of the high-κ dielectric and well-matched characteristics of n/p-FETs, the CFET inverters had ultralow gate and channel leakage currents during operation, resulting in exceptionally low Pstatic. At Vdd = 0.25 V, Pstatic is measured to be 38 fW, and even at Vdd = 1 V it remains as low as 1 pW. As summarized in Fig. 4f, the achieved Pstatic is the lowest reported among 2D material-based CMOS inverters, while simultaneously maintaining high gain.

Figure 4g compares the voltage gain values versus switch point (VM/Vdd), where VM denotes the input voltage at which Vout equals Vin. A switching point near 0.5 is critical for maximizing noise margins and ensuring symmetric logic operation. The CFET inverters demonstrated here not only achieve high voltage gains but also maintain VM/Vdd values close to the ideal 0.5. To further evaluate the noise tolerance of our CFET inverters, we estimated the noise margin (NM% = NML% + NMH%) values from the VTCs for 16 individual devices. The average NM% values are 67.5%, 82.5%, 87.5% and 89.2% at Vdd values of 0.25 V, 0.5 V, 0.75 V and 1 V, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 20), exceeding previously reported CFET implementations (Extended Data Table 1).

According to recent reports, beyond inverter operation, logic gate networks, including NAND and NOR gates, were implemented using CFET-based pull-up and pull-down configurations comprising two p-FETs and two n-FETs (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Fig. 21). Both logic gates operate reliably at a low Vdd of 0.5 V, demonstrating the feasibility of CFET-based logic beyond single-inverter circuits. The thermal stability of A-TiO2-integrated CFETs was evaluated at both material and device levels (Supplementary Note 5). The results support that the A-TiO2 dielectric and its interfaces with TMD channels retain electrical and crystallographic integrity under  back-end-of-line (BEOL) thermal conditions (up to 400 °C). However, extended high-temperature exposure beyond conventional limits causes noticeable device degradation.

It has been revealed that furthermore, the electrical performance of short-channel CFET inverters with about 50 nm channel lengths in both the bottom- and top-tier FETs was also evaluated (Extended Data Fig. 8a). The transfer characteristics of the p-FET and n-FET show well-matched threshold voltages and on-currents (Extended Data Fig. 8b). This electrical symmetry enables a high inverter voltage gain (gain = 97 V/V at Vdd = 1 V). The improvement is attributed to the higher switching current enabled by the short channels, as illustrated in the VTC and corresponding gain curve in Extended Data Fig. 8c,d. As expected, the static power consumption of these short-channel devices is higher than that of long-channel (Lch = 1 μm) CFETs, as a result of increased short-circuit current and Ioff during switching (Extended Data Fig. 8e). Further work on integrating Vth-tuning techniques is needed to achieve the critical balance of high gain and low power consumption in our CFET technology. Furthermore, we estimate dynamic power (Pdyn) (Supplementary Note 6), where the analysis indicates that the scaled CFET achieves a 39% reduction in dynamic power (Pdyn ≈ 230.3 nW, Vdd = 0.5 V), compared with the long-channel counterpart (Pdyn ≈ 378.3 nW, Vdd = 0.5 V). This improvement arises from reduced intrinsic and Miller capacitances associated with the scaled geometry, which outweighs the additional parasitic coupling introduced by the vertical stacking38,39.

In summary, this work demonstrates a 3-inch freestanding A-TiO2 membrane as a gate dielectric that delivers exceptional thickness uniformity and favourable dielectric metrics. The atomically clean interface formed between A-TiO2 and 2D materials enables low subthreshold swing, record-low hysteresis and well-balanced enhancement-mode operation for both n- and p-type transistors. Building on this gate-stack platform, vertically stacked CFET inverter arrays have high voltage gain, wide noise margins and ultralow static power consumption. Density functional theory (DFT) combined with NEGF (NEGF-DFT) simulations further project that the proposed 2D CFET architecture can be scaled to the 1-nm node while sustaining stable operation (Supplementary Note 7). Together, these results establish wafer-scale single-crystal high-κ dielectrics integrated with 2D semiconductors as viable and promising platforms for energy-efficient logic technologies, positioning them as compelling candidates for the post-silicon electronics roadmap.

The AlO2-terminated surface of single-crystalline 3-inch LaAlO3 (001) substrates was prepared by wet etching of LaAlO3 (001) for 30 s with dilute HCl (pH ≈ 4.5), followed by 1,000 °C annealing in a pure oxygen atmosphere. The atomically sharp step and terraces of substrates were examined by AFM. The SrTiO3, Sr3Al2O6 and A-TiO2 films were grown by pulsed laser deposition using a 248-nm krypton fluoride excimer laser with a laser fluence of 48 mJ cm–2. A laser-scanning system capable of depositing films on wafers up to 4-inch in diameter was used, in which a linear translation stage, rather than a galvanometer, was used to scan the laser beam across a rotating target. This configuration eliminates optical distortions and maintains consistent ablation conditions, thereby ensuring uniform film growth. The SrTiO3 buffer layer and water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 layers were deposited at 850 °C with an oxygen partial pressure (\({p}_{{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\)) of 1 × 10−6 torr. The in situ RHEED patterns indicated the highly crystalline nature for the as-grown A-TiO2 layer, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 1a). The epitaxial growth of the A-TiO2 layer on the Sr3Al2O6 thin film was then conducted at 800 °C and \({p}_{{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\) = 1 × 10−4 torr. On the completion of film deposition, the sample was cooled down to room temperature under \({p}_{{{\rm{O}}}_{2}}\) = 1 × 10−1 torr to prevent non-stoichiometry in A-TiO2 film.

The 1L-MoS2 film was synthesized via a CVD method on C/M sapphire substrates (supplied by Crystal-wise Technology), which had undergone surface reconstruction. Molybdenum trioxide (MoO3, 99.5%) and sulfur (S, 99.5%) powders (both from Sigma-Aldrich) were positioned in separate zones of a quartz tube furnace. A heating belt regulated the sulfur evaporation at 160–180 °C, whereas the substrate and MoO3 were heated to 700 °C. An argon gas flow facilitated the transport of vapourized precursors. The growth process lasted 15 min, after which the system was allowed to cool naturally to room temperature. The 2L-WSe2 film was provided by Nexstrom, where the samples were grown by CVD methods. The transfer procedures of 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 follow the common polymethyl-methacrylate-assisted wet transfer method.

Industry observers note that X-ray diffraction measurements were conducted using a Rigaku SmartLab thin-film XRD system with a rotating copper anode X-ray source. The dislocation density (\(\rho \)) is evaluated using the Vannas (Halliwell–Hirsch) model:.

where \(\beta \) is the FWHM in radians and \(b\) is the Burgers vector. The surface morphologies were examined by AFM (Bruker Dimension Icon SPM). The film thickness uniformity was measured by an ellipsometer (J.A. Woollam RC2). Raman and Photoluminescence spectra of MoS2 and WSe2 were collected in a confocal Raman microscopy system (WITec alpha 300 R) with a 532-nm laser. The cross-sectional STM measurement was conducted under ultrahigh vacuum (5 × 10−11 torr) at room temperature. Blueprint-view dark-field TEM image and SAED pattern of A-TiO2 membrane were captured using a Thermo Scientific Talos F200X STEM at 200 kV from a top-view sample suspended on a holey carbon grid. Cross-section lamellas for LaAlO3//SrTiO3//Sr3Al2O6//A-TiO2 heterostructure, single FET and CFET devices were prepared with a focused-ion-beam system (Thermo Scientific Helios 5 CX). Cross-section STEM images and EDS mapping were conducted by the same STEM system at 200 kV. The surface topography and structure of CFET logic gates were examined by SEM (Zeiss Sigma 300 VP).

For MIM capacitors, the A-TiO2 membranes were transferred onto Au-coated Si substrates; subsequently, 10 nm Ti and 80 nm Au electrodes were fabricated through the shadow mask by electron-beam evaporation. For ALD-grown amorphous dielectric oxides, we used trimethylaluminum and water as the precursors for Al2O3 deposition, whereas tetrakis (dimethylamido) hafnium and water served as the precursors for HfO2, with the growth temperature of 150 °C. For FET fabrication (Supplementary Fig. 8), the A-TiO2 membranes and 1L-MoS2/2L-WSe2 layers were sequentially transferred onto a Ti/Pt (1 nm/8 nm) local back-gate array. The channel area was defined using electron-beam lithography followed by O2 reactive-ion etching (10 mTorr, 100 W). After patterning the source/drain regions using electron-beam lithography, Sb/Au (20 nm/40 nm) and Pt/Au (5 nm/15 nm) contacts were deposited to form n-type 1L-MoS2 and p-type 2L-WSe2 FETs, respectively. The metals were deposited using thermal and e-beam evaporation, and the chamber pressure was maintained at around 10−8 Torr throughout the metal deposition process. For CFET devices (Extended Data Fig. 6), a 12-nm Au layer was first deposited on the substrate to serve as the bottom contact for the n-FET. A 1L-MoS2 film was transferred and patterned, followed by the transfer of an A-TiO2 membrane as the gate dielectric. A 10-nm Pt mid-gate was then defined on A-TiO2 to serve as the shared gate for both bottom n-FET and top p-FET. The top device was then completed by sequential transfer of a second A-TiO2 membrane and a 2L-WSe2 film, which was intentionally adopted to improve device-to-device uniformity and process tolerance during multilayer CFET fabrication, supported by independent statistical comparison of 1L-WSe2 and 2L-WSe2 devices (Supplementary Note 8). To remove surface polymer residue, a mild O2 plasma treatment (15 W, 20 s) and hot-acetone vapour (80 °C, 30 min) were applied after transferring the A-TiO2 and 2D material layers, respectively. After electron-beam lithography alignment of the active regions, 5 nm Pt/20 nm Au were deposited to form the p-FET contacts. Finally, the CFET inverter was formed by interconnecting the two pads respectively from n- and p-FETs through a via opening defined by O2/SF6 inductively coupled plasma etching, followed by Au metallization. The same via process was used for NAND and NOR logic demonstrations.

Bias-temperature instability measurements were performed at room temperature by applying gate biases of –1 V and +2 V, respectively, for 1,000 s. After removal of the stress bias, Vth recovery was monitored through transfer measurements at Vds = 1 V. The same extraction criterion was used throughout, and the Vth shift was calculated relative to the initial value as ΔVth = Vth,t – Vth,0.

It has been revealed that the transport properties of the 1L-MoS2 and 2L-WSe2 FETs were investigated using DFT combined with the NEGF formalism, as implemented in the QuantumATK package60. Here, \({V}_{\mathrm{gs}}\) and \({V}_{\mathrm{dd}}\) were set to be 0.6 V. All calculations were performed using linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO) basis set with high accuracy and PseudoDojo pseudopotential61. The exchange-correlation functional was treated at the GGA-PBE level. For the MoS2 DG-FET, a 15 × 1 × 173 Monkhorst–Pack k-point grid is used. For the 2L-WSe2 DG-FET, a 33 × 1 × 165 grid is adopted and vdW-D3 correction is used for vdW interaction62. The gate length of both devices is set to 10 nm. Two gate dielectrics are examined for electrostatic control: SiO2 with a permittivity of 3.9 and thickness of 0.9 nm, and TiO2 with a high-κ value of 25 and thickness of 5.8 nm. The atomic compensation-charge method is used to control the doping distribution in the source and drain extensions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cardiff City, Swansea City, Grimsby Town, and Iwan Morgan are all enjoying rather different fortunes in the 2026/27 campaign, but there is an interesting connection between the three clubs.

In a recent development, the two South Wales rivals are back competing at the same level again and both have plenty of reasons to be optimistic about their respective seasons. Cardiff City are rebuilding impressively following their relegation, while Swansea City are beginning to look a far more competitive outfit.

Recent findings suggest that neither has yet had the chance to get one over their rivals in the league, but that will change at the end of November when they finally meet for their first Championship clash since 2024/25. There is, however, another story they might both be keeping an eye on.

Iwan Morgan looks like a serious star in the making at Grimsby Town, with the 20-year-old already establishing himself as one of the most exciting young attacking talents in the EFL for the League Two outfit. His latest goal involvements came via a brace against Swindon Town during a 4-1 away win on Saturday.

Having left Brentford over the summer, the forward has hit the ground running, registering five goals and five assists already this season. What makes his emergence particularly interesting is his previous involvement in the academies of both Cardiff and Swansea.

He left Swansea after three years there in 2023, joining Brentford. Prior to that, the Cardiff-born forward had been with the Bluebirds for nine years. Also, these are two clubs with excellent youth-development structures and a strong reputation for giving homegrown players opportunities to establish themselves in senior football.

Morgan could quite conceivably have been starring for either side by now, or at least featuring in some capacity, but instead he is making a name for himself at Grimsby. With his performances attracting attention, both Welsh rivals could soon be left wondering how such an exciting talent slipped through their fingers.

One of the biggest frustrations for clubs developing young players is that talent can sometimes be overlooked until somebody further down the football pyramid recognises its potential.

Youngsters can be loaned out to levels that do not necessarily reflect their ability, while others are allowed to leave without ever receiving a proper opportunity in senior football.

Morgan appears to be another example of a player who might have been ready for a greater challenge much sooner. His performances suggest he is already capable of operating at League One level at the very least, despite being only 20 and playing for a Grimsby side in League Two.

Industry observers note that cardiff and Swansea may have missed their opportunity, but Grimsby's gain is enormous. They have secured a player whose ceiling could be considerably higher than the level at which they currently compete. If he helps to fire them up, he could yet be a major asset in the third tier next season.

It is not as though either Cardiff or Swansea have been particularly poor in their recent recruitment strategies. Cardiff have rebuilt impressively following relegation, adding plenty of players under the age of 25 to an existing core of academy graduates who have already demonstrated considerable quality.

In a recent development, they now boast one of the youngest squads in the Championship, with a project that has genuine potential to develop further. Swansea, meanwhile, have turned to Jamestown Analytics to help shape their recruitment under Vitor Matos.

Industry observers note that they were already becoming a more competitive and organised outfit under his management, but their recruitment has added further quality, with several signings arriving at peak or pre-peak stages of their careers. There is now a strong starting XI and enough depth on the bench to make a genuine play-off push realistic.

According to recent reports, neither club is getting everything wrong, which makes Morgan's emergence all the more frustrating. Swansea could have pushed to retain him and loan him out to a side like Grimsby. Instead, they have to watch on as he tears up the fourth tier. Both Welsh outfits will be keeping an eye on his development, though.

Goncalo Ramos is doing just about everything that can be asked of a centre-forward, except scoring goals regularly.

This morning’s Corriere dello Sport (via MilanNews) has a section headlined: ‘Now all Gonçalo needs is goals’. The Portuguese striker – who arrived at Milan in the summer for over €70m from PSG – has scored only three times so far in the league and Europa League.

Tech Report: Swansea City double transfer must be on Scott Parker's radar at West Ham

💡 Key Takeaways
  • West Ham United headed into the international break not quite where they hoped they'd be, but the Hammers remain well and truly in automatic promotion contention, as new head coach Scott Parker sets his sights on improving the squad.
  • West Ham sit just outside of the play-off places as things stand after six wins, five draws, and four defeats in their opening 15 games upon their return to the Championship.
  • Amid the club's struggles, Nuno Espírito Santo was dismissed from his post in the London Stadium dugout, swiftly being replaced by former Fulham, Bournemouth, and Burnley boss Scott Parker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

West Ham United headed into the international break not quite where they hoped they'd be, but the Hammers remain well and truly in automatic promotion contention, as new head coach Scott Parker sets his sights on improving the squad.

West Ham sit just outside of the play-off places as things stand after six wins, five draws, and four defeats in their opening 15 games upon their return to the Championship.

Amid the club's struggles, Nuno Espírito Santo was dismissed from his post in the London Stadium dugout, swiftly being replaced by former Fulham, Bournemouth, and Burnley boss Scott Parker.

Parker, who made 129 appearances for West Ham as a player once upon a time, knows exactly what the Hammers supporters demand, and having had the opportunity to assess his squad over the break, has outlined two key areas in need of improvement this winter.

According to Alan Nixon's Patreon, Parker has identified left-back and striker as the two areas West Ham must be targeting heading into the January window.

With Taty Castellanos, Pablo Felipe, and Joel Piroe as options up front right now, it's not exactly as if the Hammers are short on strength and depth in this area, but despite this, Parker is clearly not totally convinced by any of that trio as things stand.

At left-back, each of Ollie Scarles, Morato, Adam Boiro, and Ezra Mayers has covered this area of the pitch at some stage this season, though none have been able to successfully nail down a starting berth under either Nuno or Parker.

It would be no surprise to see West Ham splash the cash this winter once again to boost their promotion chances, and should look towards a fellow top-eight contender to strike a deal.

Between them, Castellanos, Pablo, and Piroe have six league goals so far this campaign, with the latter grabbing four of those, as neither Castellanos nor Pablo have been able to adapt to the Championship.

It would be no surprise to see either of those move on in the winter, either on loan or permanently, and in that event, West Ham ought to rekindle their interest in Slovenian centre-forward Zan Vipotnik.

Vipotnik, 24, finished as the Championship's top goalscorer last season, with 23 goals and three assists in 44 league appearances for Swansea City, as midway through the season, the Hammers registered an interest in the forward.

Swansea would stand firm on Vipotnik, who would eventually sign a fresh deal in South Wales, but this season, he has found himself battling for minutes with Adam Idah and Ross Stewart, as a move this winter could be on the cards.

West Ham should move again, and in the process, bring along star left-back Josh Tymon with them, with the former Hull City and Stoke City full-back a large reason for Vipotnik's goalscoring success last year.

Although Vipotnik has fallen down the pecking order at Swansea this season, his goalscoring ability at this level is undeniable, and West Ham must be looking to take advantage of his situation.

With Castellanos and Pablo likely to exit after their poor starts to the season, Vipotnik would offer a different option up top at the London Stadium, and a coach like Parker will know how to get the best out of him.

Tymon, since joining Swansea from Stoke in the summer of 2023, has cemented himself as one of the very best in his position in the entire division, especially going forward, with his excellent delivery proving incredibly difficult to defend against.

At 27 and with nearly 250 Championship appearances under his belt across his career, Tymon is in his prime years and knows the division better than most, as though neither will likely come especially cheap; if they can help guide the Hammers back to the Premier League, it would be difficult to deny they're worth it.

It has been revealed that would you like to see Vipotnik or Tymon at West Ham this January? What sort of fee would you pay for both of them? Who would be your preferred targets in these areas of the pitch? Share your thoughts below!

With a 3-3 draw away to Cardiff City and a 2-1 defeat away to Blackburn Rovers to begin his tenure as West Ham boss, Parker won't be particularly pleased with either of his sides' performances, despite battling back from 3-0 down against Cardiff.

Parker, with each of Fulham, Bournemouth, and Burnley, had the entire summer to prepare his squads for the upcoming campaign; having only ever taken charge of a club midway through the season once before with Club Brugge, this challenge poses different obstacles than what he is used to.

The Englishman will surely be aiming to stamp his authority on the West Ham side ASAP, and the additions of Vipotnik and Tymon would certainly show a statement of intent by strengthening his side and weakening a direct rival.

According to recent reports, in 2021-22 Aleksandar Mitrovic scored 43 league goals for Fulham, a Championship record. Can you beat him?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has urged caution over scrapping the 3pm blackout, and EFL clubs may have good cause to back him over this.

With rates of the illegal streaming of matches continuing to rise, there has been much conjecture in recent times over whether it is time for the ending of the 3pm blackout for televised matches.

The blackout, which prevents the broadcasting of live matches from the Premier League and the Championship between 2.45pm and 5.15pm on a Saturday, has come in for increasing criticism in recent years from fans of clubs who are unable to legally watch matches between these times while their counterparts have the ability to do so.

But now an interjection from Prime Minister Andy Burnham has cast fresh doubt over whether the blackout will be lifted in the near future, after he explained that such a decision needs to be handled carefully in order to protect smaller clubs.

Recent findings suggest that the BBC have reported that Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying that he is sceptical about the removal of the 3pm blackout. Burnham has said that he believes that any removal of the blackout should be handled extremely carefully in order to protect the revenues of smaller clubs.

Burnham has stated that, "I would urge a bit of caution [on the blackout], because it does protect the income of lower-league clubs," adding that, "If you have effectively wall-to-wall Premier League football at any time, it takes away perhaps the incentive to go and watch the football league or non-league.".

It has been revealed that do you think the 3pm blackout should remain, to protect smaller clubs? Let us know in the comments below!

Burnham, who is a long-standing supporter of Premier League club Everton, remarked that he wouldn't be taking a solely consumer-orientated view of removing the blackout: "I think it has to be considered carefully. I'm not going to take the pure consumer view here. I'll take the health-of-football approach to this particular concern.".

According to recent reports, and he also confirmed that his main aim with regard to this glitch is the protection of English football's unique pyramid system: "I think it's about protecting the experience with the paying supporter, protecting the football pyramid. Those complications matter to me, first of all.".

The 3pm blackout was first introduced in the 1960s, at a time when the televised coverage of football was first really starting to proliferate and the attitude of clubs towards the broadcasting of matches was very different to today.

At a time when match-day revenue was how clubs made the majority of their incomes, there was deep suspicion on the part of owners and chairmen about what sort of effect the widespread televising of matches might have on revenue coming into clubs.

Sources indicate that an attempt to show live Football League matches had failed in 1960 after just one match was shown, but with England hosting a World Cup in 1966 there was increased interest from broadcasters in showing matches. The Burnley chairman Bob Lord spearheaded the opposition, which resulted in the blackout being introduced. Live televised football from the Football League didn't return until October 1983.

Industry observers note that critics of the blackout argue that it is a relic from a bygone age. In an era during which matches can be illegally streamed from elsewhere in the world, they argue that allowing all matches to be shown on the television regardless of kick-off times would be beneficial to clubs, who could charge more for their rights, and for fans of massive clubs who want to see all of their teams' matches live.

The counter-argument to this is that, while no-one knows for sure what would happen were the blackout to be lifted, it's difficult to imagine a scenario in which it would be good for smaller clubs. Anecdotal evidence has long suggested that smaller clubs take a hit when they have matches scheduled for the same time as bigger matches.

Sources indicate that and it remains the case that smaller EFL clubs and non-league clubs remain more dependent on match-day revenues than bigger clubs. This isn't to say that it doesn't matter to Premier League clubs, for whom it remains their third-largest source of income. But without television deals of the value of the Premier League's or vast commercial contracts, the lower you travel down the football pyramid, the more dependent clubs are on supporters turning out for matches. A YouGov poll in 2023 found that 14% of match-going fans would be more likely to stay at home in the event that matches were shown on the television at 3pm on a Saturday.

Furthermore, supporters of retaining the ban argue that removing the blackout would be akin to letting a genie out of a bottle. The likelihood of removing the ban would be a one-way street, and even if the effects of it were more severe for smaller clubs than anticipated, the likelihood of it being reinstated would be extremely thin. And with the rights to Premier League or Championship matches still being extremely valuable, big increases to the amounts being paid for matches at that level would only further widen the financial gap between the wealthiest clubs and the rest.

Recent findings suggest that the Premier League and EFL could, if they wanted to, remove all of their matches from the period covered by the 3pm blackout and ensure that all matches could be shown live on the television. But with matches already routinely being shown at lunchtime, early in the evening, and increasingly on Saturday nights, it seems unlikely that the bigger clubs would do anything but fill in the gaps with more live televised football in the event that it was removed.

According to recent reports, andy Burnham's comments will cause a mixed reaction. The 2023 YouGov poll found that 25% of all fans supported the blackout while 52% were against it, though these numbers changed to 44% in favour and 45% against when it came to match-going fans. Balancing these opposing interests could prove tricky for the Prime Minister, given the conflicting nature of the desire of bigger clubs to maximise their revenues and smaller clubs' fears over what effect loosening or abolishing it could have upon them.

Sources indicate that if Andy Robertson’s first 101 caps for Scotland taught him anything, it’s that we have never been a nation to make life easy for ourselves. It’s in our DNA.

Why, therefore, would he have expected cap No102 to be any different?

This was meant to have been a celebration of one of Scotland’s greatest-ever servants on the night when he equalled Kenny Dalglish’s total appearances against the whipping boys of Nations League Group B1.

Industry observers note that as the cliché goes, there’s no gimmes at this level. But that’s nonsense. This is exactly what Robertson’s special night should have been. A gimme.

According to recent reports, the visitors hadn’t registered a goal yet in this campaign, never mind a point. They were rotten when Robertson and Co scored twice without reply in Skopje last month, and it was the same story for much of this forgettable contest.

According to recent reports, the problem is that Scotland weren’t much better. In the first half, at least.

Andy Robertson joined Kenny Dalglish on 102 caps as Scotland saw off North Macedonia.

Thankfully, they got the job done after the break to ensure it would be a night Robertson will look back on fondly after all.

He’s earned that too, even if his own individual performance didn’t quite hit the heights of so many that have gone before. But nobody will remember that.

According to recent reports, perhaps he knackered himself by covering what must have been around 10km in a small-sided kickabout during the warm-up. He may not have the same turn of pace in his arsenal that he possessed when he first broke into the international fold as a fresh-faced teenager. But, in terms of intensity, the 32-year-old is still an animal, in the nicest possible way. He hassled and harried every one of his team-mates throughout the pre-game stuff, barking out all sorts of instructions along the way.

In many ways, he is still the same standard-bearer he’s always been. It was a shame he couldn’t quite lead the way when the serious stuff got started.

Recent findings suggest that operating on the left-hand side of a four-man midfield, the Spurs man – as he does as frequently as ever – bombed up and down the flank all night. However, his deliveries from several promising positions weren’t quite up to scratch.

It has been revealed that A couple hit the first man. A couple cleared the upright. None caused any sort of alarm in the North Macedonian backline.

Robertson was his customary energetic self as he bombed up and down the left-hand side.

He was made to work harder than he would have liked at the other end too, as the visitors threatened to spoil the party on more than one occasion in the second 45.

In truth, he didn’t look particularly comfortable in Sebastien Pocognoli’s new-look side. Then again, few did.

The Belgian will be given plenty of time to really put his stamp on this Scotland team, but there’s no two ways about it. The early signs are uninspiring to say the least.

By the end, people got sick of the attritional style employed by Steve Clarke. Pocognoli arrived with a reputation for going with a more enterprising approach.

Really? It’s fair to say, the wait to see it in action goes on.

According to recent reports, it’s not the time to panic. But you get the sense patience is already being stretched amongst some sections of the Tartan Army.

They weren’t shy in airing their frustrations last night. Scott McTominay was on the receiving end of a few grumbles, as was Ben Gannon-Doak who once again did so much right until the all-important crucial last bit.

Yes, he may have won the winning penalty which John McGinn duly slotted away, but let’s be honest, there was more than a touch of good fortune about it.

The Scotland skipper leads his side out at Hampden on a night he will remember forever.

He should have burst the net when put clean through by Oli McBurnie long before keeper Stole Dimitrievski caught him near the byline.

According to recent reports, the Bournemouth youngster is seen by many as undroppable, and there’s merit to that argument in that Pocognoli doesn’t have anyone else like him to call upon. However, he needs to improve the final part of his game to ensure he becomes Scotland’s main man in the years to come.

Had Scotland been a few goals to the good by the time McGinn stepped up to notch his second of the night, you suspect Robertson may have fancied taking the spot-kick himself.

If only it had been that comfortable.

Still, the record books will show that Robertson’s record-equalling night will ultimately go down as a triumph for all involved, even if it didn’t feel like it at the time.

United had come into this getting battered from all sides and when Pablo Barrios put Atlético ahead, Jamie Carragher’s pre-match assessment about how things could get “very messy, very quickly” for all involved at Old Trafford must have been ringing in the ears of the travelling supporters.

Another defeat intensified the pressure on Carrick but Martínez left nobody under any illusions that he felt the finger should be pointed not simply at another manager or the players, but the hierarchy above him.

It was extraordinary to see a player speaking out so publicly in this fashion against his own bosses.

But Martínez pulled no punches, even going as far as singling out Jason Wilcox, the director of football, as he criticised the club’s summer transfer business and effectively accused the club of failing Carrick and the players in the window.

To what extent Martínez’s comments mirror the views of the wider dressing room is unclear, but you have to wonder where Carrick and United go from here.

According to recent reports, on the one hand, Martínez was providing a show of support for his manager by attacking the people above him. At the same time, he has presented Carrick with a disciplinary problem to address.

Lisandro Martínez did NOT hold back after United's loss to Atletico 😬👀 https://t.co/OGo25Pzd30.

And United have enough troubles as it is without a senior member of Carrick’s dressing room turning so squarely against the club’s power brokers.

Martínez was probably only giving voice to what many fans have been saying since an underwhelming transfer window closed with more questions than answers. But for a player to talk in such blunt, excoriating terms resonated more loudly than anything a supporter or United’s most caustic critic could say.

The message was simple: you can sack all the managers you want but until you pull together a squad worthy of United’s name and give the man at the helm the tools to compete, the club will struggle to escape this cycle of mediocrity.

No one can reasonably argue United’s window was a success. They went into it with the hopes of landing Elliot Anderson and other premium midfielders but ended up going for numbers over proven quality or pedigree. Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba were not a trio of signings anyone expected at the start of summer, not even the club itself.

There were glaring complications to address in defence, not least at left-back, and at centre-forward but a quality alternative to Luke Shaw never materialised and no back-up was signed for Benjamin Sesko, who was missing for four months with a shin injury that has since resurfaced and which could keep him out for a while yet.

Having done so well to lead United to third and take them back into the Champions League, Carrick would have expected further backing than he got in the summer. Ever the firm man, he has been too polite to criticise that lack of investment. But the cat is out of the bag now Martínez has had his say.

Industry observers note that it now places the spotlight on Wilcox. United head to Elland Road on Sunday and that was the scene of Rúben Amorim’s final meltdown as manager. Two days after he blew up in a meeting with Wilcox at United’s Carrington training base, Amorim took aim at the director of football and others at the club, demanding they “do their job” and repeatedly declaring that he had come to Old Trafford to “be the manager, not to be the coach”.

It is remarkable to think that, 10 months on, United head back to Leeds with just as many questions as there were back then.

United’s worst start to a league season for 40 years has ensured Carrick is already under pressure, but Martínez is very much of the view that it is no longer enough for the manager and the players to keep carrying the can and that the credibility and suitability of those who recruit the players and make the decisions must now be called into question.

It has been revealed that that Martínez picked this game to speak out was interesting. United, lost, yes, and the manner of Atlético’s opening goal from Barrios after 53 seconds was shocking. But United at least went down fighting on this occasion and had fashioned enough good chances to at least draw level before Yoro’s harsh 74th-minute red card swung a delicately poised match decisively in Atlético’s favour.

Lookman made it 2-0 soon after, but Atlético, having looked like they would run all over United in those opening 10 minutes, were made to work hard for their victory.

Sources indicate that united cannot keep shooting themselves in the foot like they did in the first minute. Carrick had gone with a three-man midfield to shore things up and made his team more comfortable and yet they were opened up in double quick time by two passes through the middle.

Still, you only needed to look across at United’s opponents to appreciate how chaotic it had become at Old Trafford.

Diego Simeone’s reign at Atlético covers a period stretching two years longer than the post-Ferguson era and in many ways his teams have represented everything United have not been in that time: well constructed and thought through, unified, stable, organised, hungry, aggressive, uncompromising and with a flash of devilment.

If United were not in crisis before this, they are now.

Sources indicate that good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League tie between Atlético Madrid and Manchester United from the Metropolitano. The two sides had contrasting fortunes in their opening fixtures in this competition, Man Utd beating Azerbaijan’s Sabah 4-0 at Old Trafford a month ago while Atléti were defeated by Liverpool who came back from 1-0 down to win 2-1.

But domestically it is the other way round – Michael Carrick’s side have made the club’s worst start in the league for 40 years with one win, three draws and two defeats and have been knocked out of the League Cup. Those of us who watch them regularly – purely because of occupational obligations in this instance – have been surprised by how poor they have been. The results have been bad but the performances even worse.

It has been revealed that they seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Recent findings suggest that atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

It has been revealed that the one surviving veteran in the squad from that first of El Cholo’s Liga winning sides and the two Champions League finals, victory in which would represent Simeone’s crowning achievement, is the midfielder Koke. Remarkably, if he features today, the 34-year-old midfielder will be making his 750th first-team appearance as an Atlético player.
